source.title: Where Investment Goes
source.summary: Capital allocation, the riba prohibition, real estate misallocation, and the gap between Islamic finance theory and practice.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Two countries with identical savings rates can have vastly different growth outcomes depending on how capital is allocated. The financial system channels savings into investment, and its efficiency determines growth. Capital misallocation reduces TFP in developing countries by 30 to 50 percent. Islamic economics prohibits interest, which should theoretically redirect capital: equity-based financing (mudaraba, musharaka) aligns incentives and directs capital toward productive uses rather than safe borrowers with mediocre projects. But Islamic banking in practice hasn't delivered this. Most Islamic banks use murabaha, which is economically similar to conventional lending. Genuine profit-loss sharing remains rare. Meanwhile, Muslim-majority economies suffer from massive real estate misallocation and underdeveloped equity markets. The principles are sound. The implementation gap is enormous.

thread: Capital misallocation reduces productivity by 30 to 50 percent in developing countries. Two economies with identical savings rates can have completely different growth outcomes.
Islamic finance was supposed to solve this. Equity partnerships like mudaraba align investor incentives with productive ventures rather than rewarding safe borrowers with mediocre projects.
Instead, most Islamic banks chose murabaha—economically identical to conventional lending. True profit-loss sharing remains rare across Muslim-majority economies.
The theory pointed toward better capital allocation. The practice recreated the same misallocation problems. https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-re-4

linkedin.post: Two countries with identical savings rates can have vastly different growth outcomes. The difference lies in capital allocation—how efficiently the financial system channels savings into productive investment. Capital misallocation reduces total factor productivity by 30 to 50 percent in developing countries. The financial system's efficiency in directing capital determines economic growth. Islamic economics offers a compelling alternative: equity-based financing through mudaraba and musharaka partnerships. These structures align investor incentives with productive ventures rather than simply rewarding safe borrowers with mediocre projects. Yet Islamic banking in practice hasn't delivered this transformation. Most Islamic banks rely on murabaha, which is economically similar to conventional lending. Genuine profit-loss sharing remains rare across Muslim-majority economies. The theory pointed toward better capital allocation. The practice recreated the same problems it sought to solve. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-re-4
